reference.source: ESC/AHA guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death; Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: A rare inherited channelopathy defined by an abnormally short QT interval and a high risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death
May present with palpitations, syncope, atrial fibrillation at a young age, or aborted cardiac arrest, sometimes as the first event
The ECG shows a persistently short QT interval with tall, peaked, symmetrical T waves and often a short or absent ST segment

Most identified variants are gain-of-function changes in potassium channel genes (such as KCNH2, KCNQ1 and KCNJ2) that shorten repolarisation; some loss-of-function calcium channel variants overlap with a Brugada phenotype
Diagnosis rests on the corrected QT interval together with symptoms, family history and genetic findings, as the QT alone can overlap with normal variants
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is the mainstay for those who survive cardiac arrest or are at high risk
Quinidine can prolong the QT interval and is used to reduce arrhythmic events, particularly when a defibrillator is unsuitable
Family screening is important because the first manifestation may be sudden death
reference.pathophysiology: Short QT syndrome is caused by ion channel dysfunction that accelerates cardiac repolarisation. Gain-of-function variants in potassium channel genes increase outward repolarising currents, shortening the action potential duration and thereby the QT interval; loss-of-function variants in calcium channel subunits can produce a similar phenotype. The abbreviated and heterogeneous repolarisation shortens refractory periods across the atria and ventricles, creating a substrate for re-entry that predisposes to atrial fibrillation and to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, and hence sudden death, in a structurally normal heart.
additionalDifferentials: Normal QT variant or measurement error
Effects of digoxin on the ST segment and QT
Brugada syndrome (with overlapping calcium channel variants)
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG with careful measurement of the corrected QT interval and T-wave morphology
Serial or repeat ECGs to confirm a persistently short QT
Ambulatory monitoring for atrial and ventricular arrhythmia
Correction and reassessment after excluding electrolyte and drug causes of QT shortening
Echocardiography to confirm a structurally normal heart
Genetic testing for potassium and calcium channel variants with family cascade screening
redFlags: Aborted cardiac arrest or documented ventricular fibrillation
Unexplained syncope in a young person with a short QT
Atrial fibrillation presenting at an unusually young age
Family history of sudden cardiac death
reference.prognosis: The natural history is dominated by the risk of sudden arrhythmic death, which can occur across all ages including infancy; appropriate defibrillator therapy and, where used, QT-prolonging drug therapy substantially improve outcome for high-risk individuals.
pitfalls: Overlooking a short QT interval because attention focuses on QT prolongation
Attributing a short QT to hypercalcaemia or digoxin without reassessing after correction
Relying on the QT value alone without integrating symptoms, family history and genetics
Failing to screen relatives given that sudden death can be the first event
Assuming a structurally normal heart excludes life-threatening arrhythmia
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator implantation as the mainstay for survivors of aborted cardiac arrest or those judged at high arrhythmic risk

Quinidine or another class Ia antiarrhythmic to prolong repolarisation and lengthen the QT interval, reducing ventricular arrhythmia, especially where a defibrillator is declined or unsuitable or as an adjunct to reduce shocks
Correction of electrolyte disturbances and avoidance of influences that further abbreviate repolarisation
Management of associated atrial fibrillation with rhythm or rate control and anticoagulation as indicated, exercising caution when suppressing conduction
Ambulatory and serial ECG surveillance for atrial and ventricular arrhythmia and device interrogation to guide therapy
Genetic counselling with cascade ECG and genetic screening of first-degree relatives
Prompt escalation to specialist inherited-arrhythmia review after syncope, palpitations or an appropriate device therapy
